source.how: Usage section (When to use / When not to use / Do / Don't) and the summary line of each page's newest `Documentation*` frame. Behavioural rules only: the Properties and Guideline sections are left out because they speak in Figma property names and carry prose numbers that disagree with the boards (AGENTS.md section 6).
source.legacy: Alert, Breadcrumb and Button Group have no summary line in their Documentation frame; theirs comes from the older `<Name> - Usage Doc` frame and is marked `summaryFrom: legacy`.

Avatar.summary: An avatar represents a user or entity through an image, initials, or icon, helping provide identity and context within the interface.
whenToUse: Use to identify the author of a comment, message, post, or activity entry.
Use in lists, tables, or cards to scan owner/assignee at a glance.
Use letter variant (initials on colored bg) when no photo is available.
Use number variant for grouped count indicators (e.g., “+3 more” in a stack).
Use empty variant when identity is unknown but a placeholder slot is needed.
Use error variant when an avatar fails to load or a user is invalid.
whenNotToUse: Don't use for system/non-human entities  →  use Icon
Don't use for status indicators alone  →  use Badge
Don't use as the only menu trigger  →  use Button as wrapper
Don't use at sizes below 24px  →  use Icon (initials unreadable)
do: Pick the avatar color deterministically from user id/initials so it stays stable
Use the face-centered crop for image variant
Use 1–2 uppercase letters for initials (“AB”)
Add aria-label describing the user's name
dont: Randomize avatar color on each render
Use a non-square source image without cropping
Use 3+ letters or lowercase initials
Leave avatars unannounced for screen readers

Button.summary: A button triggers an action or submits a form — the primary way users commit to a decision in a form, card, dialog, or toolbar.
whenToUse: Use for the primary action in a form, card, dialog, or toolbar.
Use one primary Button per view for the main action.
Use Secondary / Outline / Ghost for lower-emphasis actions.
Use Destructive for irreversible actions (delete, remove).
Use Icon Only in dense toolbars where space is tight.
whenNotToUse: Don't use to navigate between pages  →  use Link
Don't use for an on/off setting  →  use Toggle / Switch
Don't use for many related options  →  use Segmented control
Don't nest a Button inside another Button or Link.
do: Use one clear primary action per view
Keep labels to 1–3 words, sentence case, verb-first
Use Destructive only for irreversible actions
Provide an aria-label for Icon Only buttons
dont: Place two primary Buttons side by side
Write full sentences or ALL CAPS labels
Use vague labels like “Submit” or “OK”
Trigger destructive actions on the first click

Badge.summary: A badge is a small, color-coded label that communicates an item's status, category, or count using concise text.
whenToUse: Use to communicate the status or state of an item (e.g., Success, Waiting, Reject).
Use in tables, lists, or cards to label rows at a glance.
Use the reverse (solid) style for high-emphasis or active states.
Use the subtle style for low-emphasis, inline status.
Use the Custom variant for domain-specific states not covered by the defaults.
whenNotToUse: Don't use for interactive actions  →  use Button
Don't use to identify a person  →  use Avatar
Don't use for long text or full sentences  →  use plain text
Don't use as a count bubble on an icon  →  use Notification dot
do: Keep labels to 1–2 words in title case
Map each status to a consistent variant color
Use the icon slot only when it adds meaning
Pair color with text so meaning isn't color-only
dont: Write full sentences inside a badge
Reuse the same color for unrelated statuses
Rely on color alone to convey meaning
Stack multiple badges where one status suffices

Checkbox.summary: A checkbox lets users select one or more options from a set, or toggle a single setting on or off. It supports checked, unchecked, indeterminate, disabled, and error states.
whenToUse: Use to select one or more options from a list (multi-select).
Use to toggle a single independent setting on or off.
Use the indeterminate state for a parent of a partially-selected group.
Add a subtext for a short helper or description under the label.
whenNotToUse: Don't use for a single instant on/off  →  use Toggle
Don't use for mutually exclusive options  →  use Radio
Don't use for one pick among many  →  use Select
Don't use as a primary action  →  use Button
do: Keep labels short and describe what selecting does
Use indeterminate only on a parent of a group
Group related checkboxes vertically
Make both label and box part of the click target
dont: Write long sentences as a checkbox label
Use the checked state to trigger navigation
Rely on color alone to signal an error
Nest unrelated options under one parent

Button Link.summary: A button link is a text-only, inline action styled as a link — used for low-emphasis or navigational actions where a full button would be too heavy.
whenToUse: Use for low-emphasis or inline actions within or beside text.
Use for link-like navigation (go to a page, open a doc).
Use the Invert variant on dark or colored backgrounds.
Use Tertiary / Secondary for de-emphasized actions in dense UI.
whenNotToUse: Don't use for the primary action in a form  →  use Button
Don't use for an on/off state  →  use Toggle
Don't use as the only target in a large tap area  →  use Button
Don't mix with filled buttons in the same action row.
do: Keep labels short, verb-first, sentence case
Style links consistently so they're recognizable
Use Invert only on sufficiently dark surfaces
Provide a clear focus state for keyboard users
dont: Use vague labels like “Click here”
Style a link identical to body text (not recognizable)
Use Invert on light backgrounds (low contrast)
Stack many links where a menu would be clearer

Radio Button.summary: A radio button lets users choose exactly one option from a set. Options are mutually exclusive — selecting one clears the others in the same group.
whenToUse: Use to pick exactly one option from a short, mutually exclusive set.
Use when all options should be visible at once (2–6 items).
Use a subtext to clarify an option without leaving the list.
Use a default selection when a safe or common choice exists.
whenNotToUse: Don't use to select multiple options  →  use Checkbox
Don't use for on/off of one setting  →  use Toggle
Don't use for long option lists  →  use Select
Don't leave a group with nothing selectable.
do: Keep options in one group with a single name
Order options logically or by frequency
Keep labels parallel and concise
Make both the radio and its label clickable
dont: Leave nothing selected when a default is expected
Mix radios from different groups in one list
Use a radio to trigger an action — it sets state
Nest a radio group inside another option

Switch.summary: A switch toggles a single setting on or off, taking effect immediately. It pairs a sliding control with a label, and supports active, disabled, and error states.
whenToUse: Use to toggle a single, independent setting that takes effect immediately (e.g. Wi-Fi, notifications).
Use where the result is a binary on/off with no Save step.
Use a label that states what turning it on does.
Use the small size in dense rows or compact settings lists.
whenNotToUse: Don't use when changes need a Save  →  use Checkbox
Don't use to pick one of several options  →  use Radio
Don't use to trigger an action  →  use Button
Don't use for risky changes without a confirm step.
do: Apply the change instantly when toggled
Label for what 'on' means, not the action
Keep the switch and its label on one line
Show loading or disabled state while pending
dont: Require a separate Save after toggling
Use vague labels that hide what 'on' does
Use a switch for multi-select lists
Leave it in an ambiguous in-between state

Tag.summary: A tag is a small label that marks an item with a keyword, category, or attribute. It can carry a leading icon and an optional close button to remove it.
whenToUse: Use to label an item with a keyword, category, status, or attribute.
Use a removable tag (with close) for user-applied filters or selections.
Use a leading icon to reinforce the tag's type or meaning.
Use the outline style for a lighter, lower-emphasis label.
whenNotToUse: Don't use to trigger an action  →  use Button
Don't use for a standalone status  →  use Badge
Don't use for navigation between views  →  use Tabs
Don't use long phrases or sentences as a tag.
do: Keep labels short (1–2 words), sentence case
Show the close icon only when the tag is removable
Group related tags and let them wrap
Use a consistent variant within one group
dont: Pack a long sentence into a tag
Mix removable and static tags without a cue
Use color alone to convey meaning
Use tags as primary navigation

Tabs.summary: Tabs let users switch between related views within the same context, showing one panel at a time. They come in a segmented (pill) style and a line (underline) style.
whenToUse: Use to switch between related views or sections within one page or panel.
Use when content is peer-level and only one view shows at a time.
Use the segmented style for a small, fixed set of toggles or filters.
Use the line style for primary, section-level navigation.
whenNotToUse: Don't use for sequential steps  →  use a Stepper
Don't use for page-to-page navigation  →  use a Nav menu
Don't use to filter many options  →  use Select / Chips
Don't use when views are unrelated or hierarchical.
do: Keep exactly one tab selected at all times
Keep labels short (1–2 words) and parallel
Keep the visible panel in sync with the active tab
Limit the count so all tabs fit without scrolling
dont: Open a new page or dialog from a tab
Hide critical content behind a rarely-seen tab
Use long labels that wrap or truncate
Nest tabs inside tabs in the same view

Hint.summary: A hint is a small notification badge that signals unread or pending items — shown as a plain dot or a count, attached to an icon, tab, or menu item.
whenToUse: Use to flag unread or pending items on an icon, tab, avatar, or menu entry.
Use the dot type when only presence matters, not the exact count.
Use a digit type to show a specific count of items.
Use 99+ to cap large counts and keep the badge narrow.
whenNotToUse: Don't use to label status or category  →  use Badge
Don't use as standalone text  →  use a Badge or number
Don't use as an interactive control  →  use Button
Don't attach more than one hint to a single target.
do: Anchor the hint to the top-right of its target
Keep counts accurate and update them live
Cap counts at 99+ to keep the width stable
Announce changes to assistive tech (aria-live)
dont: Show a 0 count — hide the hint instead
Use a dot and a count at the same time
Obscure the underlying icon or label
Use it for long or multi-word text

Separator.summary: A separator is a thin line that visually divides content into groups — between list items, sections, or side-by-side elements — without adding emphasis.
whenToUse: Use to divide groups of related content (list rows, menu sections, form blocks).
Use a vertical separator between inline items in a toolbar or stat row.
Use to set a card or panel header/footer apart from its body.
Use sparingly — reach for spacing first, lines second.
whenNotToUse: Don't use just to decorate  →  use spacing
Don't stack lines for emphasis  →  use a heading
Don't put a line around every item  →  group with whitespace
Don't use as a container border  →  use a Card / stroke
do: Keep the line thin and low-contrast (1px, neutral)
Align separators to the content edges
Prefer whitespace; add a line only when grouping is unclear
Match the length to the content it divides
dont: Use heavy or colored lines for plain division
Indent separators inconsistently in a list
Separate every single row in a dense list
Use a line where a gap would read better

whenToUse: Group related content into collapsible sections — FAQs, settings, long forms — so users scan headings first and expand only what's relevant.
whenNotToUse: Don't hide critical content users always need — show it inline. Avoid deeply nesting accordions inside one another.
do: Keep titles short and descriptive. Let panel content reflow naturally. Use subtext to add brief secondary context.
dont: Don't place primary actions only inside collapsed panels. Don't disable an accordion without a clear reason.

Alert.summary: Communicate a persistent, in-page message about the status of a page, section, or action.
whenToUse: Surface a system message tied to a page or section — non-blocking feedback, a validation summary, or a status update that should stay visible.
whenNotToUse: Transient confirmation (≤5s) → use Toast. Inline field-level error → use Hint. Blocking decision → use Modal.
do: Match the variant to message severity. Keep the label ≤6 words, sentence case. Show one Alert per scope. Pair errors with a clear next step.
dont: Don't use error for non-critical messages — it cries wolf. Don't use full paragraphs as the label. Don't stack competing alerts.

whenToUse: Use to confirm a consequential or destructive action — delete, discard, sign out — where the user must explicitly decide before proceeding.
whenNotToUse: Non-blocking message → use Alert or Toast. Complex form or multi-step flow → use Modal / Dialog. Simple inline confirmation → avoid a modal entirely.
do: State the consequence clearly in the title. Use a verb for the primary button (Delete, Continue). Keep the safe choice as Cancel on the left.
dont: Don't use vague labels like OK or Yes. Don't make the destructive action the default focus. Don't stack multiple alert dialogs.

whenToUse: Wrap an image, video, map, or embed that must keep a consistent proportion as the layout resizes — preventing distortion and reflow.
whenNotToUse: Content with intrinsic, variable height (text blocks, lists). Cases where the exact pixel size is fixed and known — size it directly instead.
do: Place a single media element in the slot and let it fill. Pick the ratio that matches the source media. Use inside responsive grids and cards.
dont: Don't put multiple unrelated elements in one Aspect Ratio. Don't override the height manually — let the ratio drive it.

Breadcrumb.summary: Show the user's location within a hierarchy and let them navigate back to any ancestor level.
whenToUse: Use on pages nested two or more levels deep so users can see where they are and jump back to any parent section.
whenNotToUse: Flat sites with a single level. As primary navigation — breadcrumbs complement, not replace, the main nav. For linear flows → use a Stepper.
do: Show the full path from home to the current page. Make every level except the current one a link. Collapse long trails with an ellipsis.
dont: Don't make the current page a link. Don't wrap the trail onto two lines — collapse with the ellipsis instead. Don't omit the home level.

Button Group.summary: Group related action buttons horizontally so they share borders and read as one control.
whenToUse: Present a short, fixed set of related choices or page numbers as one connected control — pagination, view toggles, segmented filters.
whenNotToUse: A single action → use Button. Many pages (>9) → use Pagination with ellipsis. Unrelated actions that shouldn't read as one control.
do: Keep the count small and labels short. Group only related items. Mark the active item as selected. Use 9+ for ranges beyond nine.
dont: Don't mix unrelated actions in one group. Don't exceed nine items — use the 9+ overflow. Don't use it for a page's primary action.

whenToUse: Capture a date, date range, or time. Use the desktop Calendar for inline selection; on mobile use the Popup for compact fields or the Drawer for full-width bottom-sheet selection.
whenNotToUse: A single known date that's faster to type. Avoid a Drawer on desktop or an inline Calendar on small mobile screens — match the picker to the breakpoint.
do: Match the platform — D- for desktop, M- for mobile. Offer presets for common ranges, and provide a Reset to clear the selection.
dont: Don't mix desktop and mobile variants in one breakpoint. Don't hide the selected value. Don't omit AM/PM where 12-hour time is expected.

Carousel.summary: A carousel displays a set of items in a scrollable horizontal or vertical track, with previous/next navigation buttons and a position indicator. It supports multiple content aspect ratios.
whenToUse: Use to browse a set of related images or cards in a confined space.
Use Horizontal for wide, gallery-style content; Vertical for stacked feeds.
Use the aspect ratio that matches the media (16:9 video, 1:1 thumbnails, 9:16 stories).
Use the indicator so users know their position within the set.
Use navigation buttons on pointer surfaces where swipe is not available.
whenNotToUse: Don't mix different aspect ratios within a single carousel.
Don't hide both the buttons and the indicator at once.
Don't overload one carousel with too many items.
Don't use a carousel for primary navigation  →  use Tabs or a List.
do: Keep slot content uniform in size and aspect ratio.
Show at least the active plus an adjacent item to hint scrollability.
Pair the indicator with buttons for accessible navigation.
Keep one consistent aspect ratio across all slots.
dont: Mix aspect ratios within one carousel.
Hide both navigation buttons and the indicator.
Cram too many items into a single carousel.
Use it as the only way to reach important content.

whenToUse: Group related information and actions into a self-contained block — summaries, list items, dashboard tiles, or media previews.
whenNotToUse: A single line of text or a plain layout container with no grouping purpose. Avoid deeply nesting cards inside cards.
do: Keep one clear subject per card. Use the footer for the card's primary and secondary actions. Use the Image type for media-led content.
dont: Don't overload a card with unrelated actions. Don't put more than two footer buttons. Don't stretch the Small type with long content.

whenToUse: Visualize quantitative data — comparisons (bar), trends over time (line), or part-to-whole proportions (pie/doughnut). Wrap in the Chart container for a titled card.
whenNotToUse: A few values better shown as text or a table. Pie charts for more than ~5 slices or precise comparisons — use a bar chart instead.
do: Pick the chart type that fits the data question. Keep color usage consistent across series. Add value labels when exact figures matter.
dont: Don't mix unrelated series in one chart. Don't use 3D or decorative effects. Don't omit axis labels on bar and line charts.

whenToUse: Focus the user on one guided task — a short form, a confirmation, or a step that needs a title, brief instruction, and clear primary / secondary actions.
whenNotToUse: For long multi-step flows → use a full page or wizard. For passive status messages → use Alert or Toast, not a blocking panel.
do: Lead with a clear title and one-line subtext. Keep the body slot focused. Make the primary action obvious and the secondary a safe exit.
dont: Don't cram many fields or steps into one panel. Don't hide the close affordance. Don't make both footer buttons look primary.

whenToUse: Show contextual details, forms, or settings without leaving the page — filters, record details, create / edit flows. Right drawer on desktop, bottom sheet on mobile.
whenNotToUse: For critical confirmations → use Alert Dialog. For full, complex workflows → use a dedicated page. Don't stack multiple drawers on top of each other.
do: Match the platform — D- right drawer on desktop, M- bottom sheet on mobile. Keep a clear title, a close affordance, and footer actions. Use Wide only when content needs it.
dont: Don't hide the close affordance. Don't overload a drawer with unrelated content. Don't make the drawer wider than the content needs.

whenToUse: Let users pick from a set of options without taking up persistent space — select fields, filters, action menus, or autocomplete suggestions.
whenNotToUse: For 2–3 options that fit inline → use Radio or a segmented control. For app navigation → use a Menu or Nav, not a data dropdown.
do: Keep labels short and scannable. Add search (Combobox) for long lists. Enable scroll past ~7–8 items. Show a clear Not Found state for empty results.
dont: Don't pack dozens of items without search or scroll. Don't mix unrelated actions and data options. Don't auto-select an item on hover.

Input With Label.summary: A single-line text input with an inline label placed to the left, right, or both sides of the field. It supports icons, validation, and the same interaction states as InputField.
whenToUse: Use when the label must sit inline with the field to save vertical space.
Use L Label for a leading label (e.g. "Name:").
Use R Label for a trailing label or unit-like suffix.
Use L R Label when both a leading label and trailing element are needed.
Use validation text to guide correction inline.
whenNotToUse: Don't use when the label is long  →  use a stacked InputField with a top label.
Don't use for choosing from a fixed set  →  use InputDropdown.
Don't use for dates/times  →  use InputDate / InputTime.
Don't rely on the placeholder as the label.
do: Keep inline labels short (one or two words).
Align label and field baselines.
Show validation text close to the field, on error.
Use a consistent 16px icon size.
dont: Use long sentences as an inline label.
Use red borders without an explanatory message.
Mix label positions inconsistently across a form.
Disable a field without making the reason clear.

Input Field.summary: A single-line text input for collecting short free-form values. It supports leading/trailing icons, validation messaging, and multiple interaction states.
whenToUse: Use to collect short, single-line text such as name, email, or code.
Use a leading icon to signal the input's purpose (e.g. search, user).
Use a trailing icon for clear/reveal actions.
Use validation text to guide correction inline.
Use the disabled state when the field is not editable in the current context.
whenNotToUse: Don't use for long, multi-line text  →  use InputTextArea.
Don't use for choosing from a fixed set  →  use InputDropdown.
Don't use for dates or times  →  use InputDate / InputTime.
Don't place critical instructions only in the placeholder.
do: Always pair the field with a visible Title/label.
Keep placeholder text as an example, not an instruction.
Show validation text close to the field, on error.
Use a consistent icon size (16px) for leading/trailing icons.
dont: Rely on placeholder alone as the label.
Use red borders without an explanatory validation message.
Mix icon sizes or styles across fields.
Disable a field without making the reason clear.

Input Text Area.summary: A multi-line text input for collecting longer free-form content. It supports a character counter, validation, optional icons, a scrollbar, and the same interaction states as InputField.
whenToUse: Use to collect longer, multi-line text such as notes, descriptions, or comments.
Use the character counter to communicate a length limit.
Use validation text to guide correction inline.
Use the scroll variant when content can exceed the visible area.
Use the disabled state when the field is not editable.
whenNotToUse: Don't use for short, single-line values  →  use InputField.
Don't use for choosing from a fixed set  →  use InputDropdown.
Don't use for rich/formatted content  →  use InputRichEditor.
Don't hide the character limit until it is exceeded.
do: Always pair the field with a visible Title/label.
Show the character counter when a limit applies.
Show validation text close to the field, on error.
Allow vertical resize/scroll for long content.
dont: Rely on placeholder alone as the label.
Use red borders without an explanatory message.
Let content overflow without a scrollbar.
Disable a field without making the reason clear.

InputRichEditor.summary: A rich-text editor input with a formatting toolbar for entering styled, multi-line content. It supports leading/trailing icons, a scrollbar, validation, and the same interaction states as InputField.
whenToUse: Use to author formatted content (bold, lists, links) such as descriptions or articles.
Use the toolbar to expose common text-formatting actions.
Use the scroll variant for long content.
Use validation text to guide correction inline.
Use the disabled state when the content is read-only.
whenNotToUse: Don't use for short plain text  →  use InputField.
Don't use for unformatted multi-line text  →  use InputTextArea.
Don't use when markup output is not supported downstream.
Don't overload the toolbar with rarely-used actions.
do: Keep the toolbar to the most common formatting actions.
Show validation text close to the field, on error.
Allow the editor to grow or scroll for long content.
Preserve pasted formatting where it is safe to do so.
dont: Rely on the placeholder alone as the label.
Use red borders without an explanatory message.
Let content overflow without a scrollbar.
Disable the editor without making the reason clear.

InputFieldUnit.summary: A composite input pairing a leading unit selector (dropdown) with a text/number field. Use it for values that carry a unit — e.g. amount + currency, weight + unit. It supports validation and the same interaction states as InputField.
whenToUse: Use for a value plus a selectable unit (e.g. 10 + kg, 100 + USD).
Use the leading dropdown to choose the unit.
Use the field for the numeric/text value.
Use validation text to guide correction inline.
Use the disabled state when the value is not editable.
whenNotToUse: Don't use when there is no unit  →  use InputField.
Don't use for choosing only from a set  →  use InputDropdown.
Don't put the unit inside the value field as text.
Don't hide which part is editable.
do: Keep the unit list short and relevant.
Align the dropdown and field heights.
Show validation text close to the field, on error.
Default the unit to the most common choice.
dont: Rely on the placeholder alone as the label.
Use red borders without an explanatory message.
Mix unrelated units in one selector.
Disable a field without making the reason clear.

InputSearch.summary: A search input with a leading search icon and an optional clear action. Use it to filter or look up content. It is compact (40px) and supports validation and interaction states.

summaryCorrection.why: Known prose error: the InputSearch board is 44px (AGENTS.md section 6).

whenToUse: Use to filter a list, table, or page of content.
Use the leading search icon as the affordance.
Use a trailing clear icon to reset the query.
Use validation text for query constraints when needed.
Use the disabled state when search is unavailable.
whenNotToUse: Don't use for general text entry  →  use InputField.
Don't use for selecting from a set  →  use InputDropdown.
Don't remove the search icon affordance.
Don't hide results behind an extra submit step when live search fits.
do: Keep the search icon visible as the affordance.
Show a clear (×) action once a query is entered.
Debounce live search to avoid excess requests.
Keep the field compact and inline with content.
dont: Rely on the placeholder alone as the label where context is unclear.
Use red borders without an explanatory message.
Block typing while results load.
Disable search without making the reason clear.

Kbd.summary: A Kbd (keyboard key) is a small inline chip that represents a single physical key or shortcut token — like Ctrl or ⇧ — used to document keyboard shortcuts.
whenToUse: Use to render keyboard keys and shortcuts inline — in menus, tooltips, help text, or command palettes (e.g. Ctrl + K). Combine several Kbd chips for a key combo.
whenNotToUse: Don't use as an interactive button — it's a display token, not a control. Don't use it for general inline code or labels; use a code style or badge instead.
do: Use the Icon variant for modifier keys (⇧ ⌘ ⌥) and Text for named keys. Pick Light=No on dark surfaces so the chip stays legible. Match the platform's key conventions.
dont: Don't cram long words into a single key chip — keep each Kbd to one key or short token. Don't mix Light=Yes and Light=No chips in the same shortcut.

Modal.summary: A modal is a focused overlay dialog that interrupts the current flow to present information or request a decision, blocking interaction with the page behind it until dismissed. Available for desktop and mobile.
whenToUse: Use a modal for focused, decision-critical tasks that must interrupt the flow: confirmations, short forms, or important information the user must acknowledge before continuing.
whenNotToUse: Don't use for long forms or multi-step flows — use a dedicated page or drawer. Don't use for non-blocking, dismissible feedback — use a Toast, Alert, or inline message instead.
do: Lead with a clear title and a primary action. Pick a Size that fits the content (Small for confirmations, Large for richer content). On mobile, stack actions full-width with the primary on top.
dont: Don't stack multiple modals or remove the close affordance for dismissible dialogs. Don't overflow the modal with content that scrolls excessively — move it to a full page.

Navigation Menu.summary: The navigation menu is the top-level horizontal bar that anchors a desktop app — pairing the brand logo with primary navigation links and utilities (search, profile) so users can orient and move between sections.
whenToUse: Use as the persistent top-level navigation for a desktop application — anchoring the brand, exposing primary sections, and housing global utilities like search and the user profile.
whenNotToUse: Don't use for in-page section switching — use Tabs.
Don't use on mobile layouts — use the mobile navigation pattern (bottom bar or hamburger drawer) instead of this desktop bar.
do: Keep navigation labels short and stable.
Highlight the active section clearly.
Use Tab Style when sections behave like switchable views, and Menu when they are distinct destinations.
dont: Don't overcrowd the bar with too many top-level links — group secondary items into a menu or slot. Don't hide critical destinations behind search only.

Popover.summary: A popover is a small floating panel anchored to a trigger, used to surface contextual content — a short form, details, or controls — on click, without navigating away from the current view.
whenToUse: Use to present focused, interactive content next to a trigger — a quick edit form, filters, or extra details — that the user acts on and dismisses without leaving the page.
whenNotToUse: Don't use for plain text hints — use a Tooltip. Don't use for blocking, decision-critical flows — use a Modal. Don't pack a long, scrolling form into a popover.
do: Keep the content short and self-contained. Anchor the popover to its trigger and dismiss it on outside click or Esc. Give a clear title when the content needs context.
dont: Don't stack popovers or open one from inside another. Don't rely on it for content the user must not miss — it dismisses easily and isn't available on touch hover.

Scroll.summary: The scroll component is the thin scrollbar indicator shown alongside an overflowing container, signalling that more content is available and how far the user has scrolled.
whenToUse: Shown automatically on a scrollable container to indicate overflow and scroll position. Use Vertical for tall content, Horizontal for wide content like tables or carousels.
whenNotToUse: Don't add a scrollbar to content that fits without overflow. Don't use it as a draggable progress or range control — use a Slider for that.
do: Keep the bar subtle and let it fade when idle. Size the thumb to reflect the proportion of visible content. Use Mirror for right-to-left layouts or left-edge scrollbars.
dont: Don't make the bar so thin it's hard to grab, or so prominent it competes with content. Don't hide it entirely where users rely on it to gauge length.

Slider.summary: A slider lets users select a value or range by dragging a handle along a track, giving direct, continuous control over a bounded numeric input.
whenToUse: Use for selecting a value or range within a known min–max where approximate, visual adjustment is natural — volume, brightness, price range, zoom.
whenNotToUse: Don't use when an exact number matters — use a number input. Don't use for a small set of discrete options — use a segmented control or radio group.
do: Show the current value near the handle, and use Range when both a lower and upper bound are needed. Provide a sensible default position.
dont: Don't use the Destructive variant for routine adjustments — reserve it for values with damaging consequences. Don't make the track so short that precise control is hard.

Toggle.summary: A toggle is a two-state button that switches an option on or off. Use it standalone, or grouped in a ToggleGroup for a set of related single- or multi-select options.
whenToUse: Use a single Toggle for an on/off state tied to one option (bold, mute). Use a ToggleGroup for a related set — single-select like a view switcher, or multi-select like text formatting.
whenNotToUse: Don't use for a binary setting in a form — use a Switch. Don't use for mutually exclusive options that need labels and descriptions — use radio buttons.
do: Use a clear icon or short label so the toggled option is obvious. Keep the active state visually distinct. Use a consistent Variant and Size across a group.
dont: Don't mix Default and Outline variants within one group. Don't rely on color alone to show the active state — pair it with the filled background and label weight.

Tooltip.summary: A tooltip is a small dark overlay that appears on hover or focus to give a short, contextual hint about an element, with an arrow pointing back to its trigger.
whenToUse: Use to give a brief, supplementary hint on hover or focus — naming an icon button, clarifying a truncated label, or explaining a control.
whenNotToUse: Don't use for essential information or actions — it's hidden until hover and unavailable on touch. For rich interactive content use a Popover; for confirmations use a Modal.
do: Keep it short — a phrase or one sentence. Point the arrow (Variant) toward the trigger and position it so it doesn't cover the element it describes.
dont: Don't pack paragraphs, multiple actions, or critical controls into a tooltip. Don't trigger it on elements that aren't interactive or focusable.

Tree.summary: A tree displays hierarchical data as nested, expandable rows — files and folders, categories, or org structures — letting users drill into nested levels while keeping their place.
whenToUse: Use for hierarchical data the user navigates by expanding and collapsing — file explorers, nested categories, org charts, or a settings navigator.
whenNotToUse: Don't use for flat, non-hierarchical lists — use a List or Table. Don't nest so deeply that rows become unreadable; cap the depth or paginate.
do: Show a clear expand/collapse affordance on parent rows. Indent consistently per level and keep the selected row highlighted. Use checkboxes only when multi-select is needed.
dont: Don't mix selection and expansion into one ambiguous click target. Don't hide whether a row has children — always show the chevron when it does.
